# Pariññāvāra (Ya 4.3)
**ID:** Ya 4.3
**Section:** Yamaka (ya)
**Collection:** Abhidhamma
**Title (Pali):** Pariññāvāra
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ya4.3

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Pariññāvāra* (Ya 4.3) is the third section of the fourth chapter of the *Yamaka*, the sixth book of the Abhidhamma Piṭaka [SuttaCentral; Norman 1983; Anderson 1999]. In the architectural framework of the *Yamaka*, chapters are typically organized into three primary divisions: the delimitation of designations (*paññatti-vāra*), the process section (*pavatti-vāra*), and the comprehension or penetration section (*pariññāvāra*) [Norman 1983; Anderson 1999; Ronkin 2005]. As the concluding division of the chapter, the *Pariññāvāra* examines the extent or degree to which a given individual or class of beings comprehends or penetrates the doctrinal category under analysis [Norman 1983; Anderson 1999].
In this analytical division, the inquiry centers on the verb *parijānāti* ("to know accurately" or "to comprehend") [Anderson 1999]. Doctrinally, penetration (*pariññā*) denotes penetrating insight at the moment of entering into one of the four stages of holiness or noble attainment [Nyanatiloka 1938]. The exposition employs the characteristic paired interrogative method of the *Yamaka*, evaluating whether comprehension of one factor entails comprehension of another across a temporal sequence of present, past, and future [Nyanatiloka 1938; Anderson 1999]. Norman notes that the *Yamaka*, seemingly composed for practitioners who have already studied the Abhidhamma system and seek full competence in it, is perhaps the latest book in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka [Norman 1983].
No cross-language parallels in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan are identified for this text [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records one modern translation in one language [SuttaCentral]. According to automated text-reuse analysis by DharmaNexus, the text shares seven passages (396 characters) with the corresponding *Pariññāvāra* section of the *Anusayayamaka* (Ya 7.2.4), illustrating the modular and highly standardized doctrinal formulas applied across the divisions of the *Yamaka* [DharmaNexus; Nyanatiloka 1938].
